bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Structural dependence on coal-based thermal generation amid India's energy transition — The Company must navigate regulatory, environmental and market challenges inherent to coal-based thermal power generation in India, including the sector-wide transition toward cleaner energy, which management explicitly names as a strengthened focus area for its Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) processes in FY 2025-26.
- Geopolitical uncertainty affecting fuel supply chains — Management states it strengthened ERM processes in FY 2025-26 specifically to address geopolitical uncertainties affecting fuel supply chains, indicating this is viewed as a material and evolving risk to the Company's coal-dependent generation model.
- Fuel cost volatility — Executives are described as overseeing 'operational vulnerabilities such as fuel cost changes' as part of the Company's risk culture, reflecting the direct sensitivity of thermal generation economics to coal price movements.
- Equipment performance / operational reliability risk — Equipment performance is separately flagged (alongside fuel cost and safety metrics) as an operational vulnerability actively monitored by station leadership, underscoring the criticality of plant availability and reliability to a capital-intensive thermal generation business.
- Broad, multi-dimensional enterprise risk exposure — The Company's ERM framework explicitly classifies risks as strategic, tactical and operational, with potential financial, operational, safety, legal, reputational or strategic impact, and requires ongoing Board-level oversight via the Risk Management Committee and four dedicated sub-committees (M&A Risk, Legal/Regulatory & Tax Risk, Reputation Risk, and Commodity Price Risk), indicating the Company itself treats its risk exposure as broad and multi-dimensional rather than confined to a single category.

outlook.body: APL is undertaking a major brownfield-and-greenfield expansion of its own and its subsidiaries' thermal power generation capacity, developing 13 projects with a combined capacity of 23,720 MW, planned for completion by FY 2031-32, taking total combined capacity from 18,150 MW to 41,870 MW. The programme comprises 28 units of 800 MW capacity using Ultra-supercritical technology and 2 units of 660 MW capacity using Supercritical technology; of this, 14,120 MW is coming up at brownfield sites and 9,600 MW at greenfield sites. The Company states it possesses 100% of the land required and has placed advance orders with key equipment suppliers for boilers, turbines and generators across the entire programme, and has tied up 13,320 MW of the upcoming capacity under long-term Power Supply Agreements (PSAs) with state DISCOMs. New long-term PSAs signed during FY26 include: Assam Power Distribution Company Limited (APDCL) for the entire 3,200 MW (4x800 MW) greenfield Ultra-Supercritical plant to be built in Assam (Chapar) on a Design-Build-Finance-Own-Operate (DBFOO) basis using SHAKTI-linked coal; Bihar State Power Generation Company Limited (BSPGCL), on behalf of North and South Bihar DISCOMs, for a 2,400 MW (3x800 MW) greenfield USCTPP at Pirpainti, Bihar, also on DBFOO/SHAKTI terms; and Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) for 1,500 MW (net) of power over 25 years from a 1,600 MW greenfield USCTPP at Mirzapur, UP, on a DBFOO basis. risks.risk: Structural dependence on coal-based thermal generation amid India's energy transition
risks.note: The Company must navigate regulatory, environmental and market challenges inherent to coal-based thermal power generation in India, including the sector-wide transition toward cleaner energy, which management explicitly names as a strengthened focus area for its Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) processes in FY 2025-26.

risks.risk: Geopolitical uncertainty affecting fuel supply chains
risks.note: Management states it strengthened ERM processes in FY 2025-26 specifically to address geopolitical uncertainties affecting fuel supply chains, indicating this is viewed as a material and evolving risk to the Company's coal-dependent generation model.

Executives are described as overseeing 'operational vulnerabilities such as fuel cost changes' as part of the Company's risk culture, reflecting the direct sensitivity of thermal generation economics to coal price movements.

Equipment performance is separately flagged (alongside fuel cost and safety metrics) as an operational vulnerability actively monitored by station leadership, underscoring the criticality of plant availability and reliability to a capital-intensive thermal generation business.

The Company's ERM framework explicitly classifies risks as strategic, tactical and operational, with potential financial, operational, safety, legal, reputational or strategic impact, and requires ongoing Board-level oversight via the Risk Management Committee and four dedicated sub-committees (M&A Risk, Legal/Regulatory & Tax Risk, Reputation Risk, and Commodity Price Risk), indicating the Company itself treats its risk exposure as broad and multi-dimensional rather than confined to a single category.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Adani Power Limited (APL), headquartered in Ahmedabad, generates electricity primarily through coal-based thermal power plants and a solar facility spread across eight Indian states, and exports power to Bangladesh under a long-term Power Purchase Agreement signed with the Bangladesh Power Development Board in 2017. Its business model combines long-term PPAs with selectively positioned open capacity, and it predominantly caters to business-to-business (B2B) clients such as state government utilities and distribution companies (DISCOMs).

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Rising India power demand driven by industrialisation, urban expansion and rising energy intensity, with structural demand emerging from electric mobility, data centres and manufacturing-led growth.
- Renewable energy's variable nature is increasing the need for dependable, flexible thermal generation to balance supply and maintain grid stability, even as renewables continue to scale rapidly.
- Coal is expected to remain the backbone of India's baseload power despite the renewable push, with thermal plants increasingly transitioning to flexible operation to manage peak demand.
- India's total installed capacity is projected to reach 900 GW by 2032, with power demand growing at a 4-6% CAGR and peak demand at a faster 6-8% CAGR through FY2029-30/2032, driven by rising appliance usage, EV adoption and AI-focused data-centre load growth.
- Industry-leading EBITDA margins of around 38% in the thermal segment reflect the Company's ability to convert operating scale into sustained performance.
- Management describes a 'secured expansion pipeline' with 'long-term offtake visibility' underpinning near-term growth.
- Land availability has been secured and ordering of critical equipment (boiler, turbine and generator packages) completed for the entire expansion pipeline.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:

- No domestic coal shortage; only shipping/bunker cost uptick on imports (passed through).

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: APL is undertaking a major brownfield-and-greenfield expansion of its own and its subsidiaries' thermal power generation capacity, developing 13 projects with a combined capacity of 23,720 MW, planned for completion by FY 2031-32, taking total combined capacity from 18,150 MW to 41,870 MW. The programme comprises 28 units of 800 MW capacity using Ultra-supercritical technology and 2 units of 660 MW capacity using Supercritical technology; of this, 14,120 MW is coming up at brownfield sites and 9,600 MW at greenfield sites. The Company states it possesses 100% of the land required and has placed advance orders with key equipment suppliers for boilers, turbines and generators across the entire programme, and has tied up 13,320 MW of the upcoming capacity under long-term Power Supply Agreements (PSAs) with state DISCOMs. New long-term PSAs signed during FY26 include: Assam Power Distribution Company Limited (APDCL) for the entire 3,200 MW (4x800 MW) greenfield Ultra-Supercritical plant to be built in Assam (Chapar) on a Design-Build-Finance-Own-Operate (DBFOO) basis using SHAKTI-linked coal; Bihar State Power Generation Company Limited (BSPGCL), on behalf of North and South Bihar DISCOMs, for a 2,400 MW (3x800 MW) greenfield USCTPP at Pirpainti, Bihar, also on DBFOO/SHAKTI terms; and Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) for 1,500 MW (net) of power over 25 years from a 1,600 MW greenfield USCTPP at Mirzapur, UP, on a DBFOO basis. At the individual-plant level, Raipur TPP's Phase II expansion (two 800 MW ultra-supercritical units) is at an advanced stage with 54% progress and main plant equipment ordering initiated; Raigarh TPP's Phase II expansion (two 800 MW ultra-supercritical units) is 38% complete, a Phase III expansion (2x800 MW) received its Terms of Reference on 6 December 2025, and a dedicated railway line for the site is targeted for completion by June 2026. Separately, the Company completed the acquisition of Vidarbha Industries Power Limited (VIPL) during FY26 -- a 2x300 MW (600 MW) thermal plant at Butibori, Nagpur, Maharashtra -- through the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC, following NCLT (Mumbai) approval of the resolution plan; the Company has also expressed interest in acting as an 'Implementing Entity' for acquiring certain power assets of Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL), subject to necessary approvals, as part of a resolution plan submitted by group entity Adani Enterprises Limited under JAL's ongoing CIRP.
